Among the goods the sawmill ordered through the post office this season, one came in a quantity that is hard to account for.

#recent#, families downriver came to this paper to say their well water was not right. This paper followed the trail to the sawmill.
#weather#, three households downriver stopped drinking from their own wells. This paper followed the river upstream, to the sawmill owned by {culprit}.

neutral: The river runs past the sawmill's gate, and below it lie the wells of several households. This paper has spent the past weeks walking its banks.

neutral.t: The sawmill owned by {culprit.full} ordered forty sacks of lime this season. This paper set out to learn where the lime went.

neutral: A few households along the river have had one worry on their minds lately. This paper went and asked.
This paper has spent several weeks following a matter between the sawmill and the families downriver.

hot.t: Families downriver have been drinking bitter water for weeks, and no one has told them why. This paper will: the trouble starts at the sawmill owned by {culprit}.
Someone has been pouring something into the river, and the children downriver drink from that river every day.
What are the children downriver drinking? {culprit.full} ought to come and taste it.

lime.note: {culprit} ordered forty sacks of lime through the post office, more than the sawmill could ever use
prose: {culprit} ordered forty sacks of lime by mail this month, far more than the sawmill ordinarily uses.
{culprit} placed a single order for forty sacks of lime. Lime is commonly used to cover the smell of waste.
the sawmill took delivery of forty sacks of lime in one order, and the order was placed by {culprit}.

prose.t: !This paper looked at the order slips at the post office: {culprit} ordered forty sacks of lime this month. The sawmill does not ordinarily use that much in a year.

detail.t: A rut runs from the back gate of the sawmill to the water's edge, worn by the wheels of a loaded barrow.
Those households now fetch their water from the public well on the east side of town, half an hour there and back.
In other years the sawmill has ordered five or six sacks of lime at most.

calm.t: The sawmill keeps some forty families in this town in work, and that is a fact. The well water downriver is a fact as well.
Well water can go bad for any number of reasons. This paper notes only that every well that has gone bad lies below the sawmill.

neutral.t: A sawmill ordering lime is nothing strange. Forty sacks is. The mill's work cannot use so much, and the mill has not said where the rest went.
The wells are downstream, and the waste went into the river upstream. Set side by side, the two leave this paper no third explanation.

neutral: The sawmill is the largest employer in town, and the largest advertiser in this paper. This paper printed the story anyway, because the families downriver take the Gazette too.

hot.t: Had it been clean water, it could have been poured out by daylight. Whoever chose the night knew why.
Everybody knows whose pocket the mill's profits go into. What goes into the river, the whole town drinks.
The children downriver have drunk bitter water for a whole season, and nobody has come to say sorry.

any.t: Forty sacks of lime were ordered, and the wells taste of lime. The figure on the order slip and the taste of the water agree, and that is why this paper prints the story.
For the dumping, this paper has given its sources above. As for money slipped to the state inspector, this paper asked, and nobody could say on what day or how much. That remains a rumor.
Bad well water shows only that something is wrong with the water, not whose doing it is. This paper prints it to ask the sawmill to say what it lets into the river.
One sack of lime will whitewash a room. Forty sacks would whitewash every wall at the sawmill ten times over.
The order went through the post office, with the name, the quantity and the date written on it. That needs no witness.
The owner gave the order to dump at night, and the men who did it were paid for their work. The question belongs to the one who gave the order.

denied.t: {target.short} says the sawmill's drainage has always been done properly.
{target.short} says the lime was for whitewashing the mill and keeping off insects.
{target.short} says the wells went bad because of the dry weather.

calm.t: This paper will ask again when the wells downriver are fit to drink.

hot.t: How much longer will the river stink?

prose: {debtor} took the family mantel clock to be pawned at a shop near the railway station.
{debtor} was seen carrying a clock into the pawnshop.
the mantel clock is gone from the parlor of {debtor}, and the ticket for it is at the shop behind the station.

!There is another story, too, that {debtor} lost the money at cards.

detail.t: The clock went to the pawnshop for three dollars; getting it back will cost four.
The most recent entry in the credit book is two pounds of salt, last week.

calm: There is no shame in owing money; everyone runs short in times like these. But the storekeeper who gives credit has a living to make too.

calm.t: When the clock goes to the pawnshop, a household's circumstances are plain to see.

neutral.t: Still buying on credit after half a year means this is no passing shortage. Every month the storekeeper waits is another month of stock paid for out of the store's own pocket.
The clock was pawned for three dollars and will cost four to redeem. Short three dollars going in, a dollar more is needed coming out: the longer it goes on, the more it costs.

neutral: This paper does not print the matter to make anyone a laughingstock. If the general store goes under, there will be nowhere left in town to buy a pound of flour on credit.

hot.t: A poor family owes thirty cents and the storekeeper is at the door the next day. A person of standing owes for half a year, and no one says a word.
Even the clock has gone to the pawnshop, and still the show of money goes on in public.

any.t: An account left standing at the store, a clock left at the pawnshop: the two say the same thing. There has not been enough ready money in that household for some time.

As for the talk that these are gambling debts, everyone this paper asked had only heard it, and not one had seen a card table. The store account is written in a book. The two are not to be added together.
One of the town's most respectable people owes the general store, and the storekeeper is too embarrassed even to knock at the door.
What {target.short} says carries weight in this town. So do the figures in that account book.
Half a year without a payment, and more goods taken on credit all the while. Kept up that long, the store is no longer selling; it is lending.
The credit book is kept by the store itself, and the one who owes could dispute it. Yet in half a year, nobody has come forward to say the book is wrong.
People who pawn things mostly mean to redeem them. A clock pawned and not redeemed means the money has stayed short.

denied: {target.short} says the matter is private, between debtor and store, and no concern of a newspaper's.

denied.t: {target.short} says the account will be settled sooner or later.
{target.short} says the clock was {target.his} own, and whether to pawn it was a family matter.

calm.t: This paper will ask again when the account is paid.

calm: This is a private matter between two households, and this paper would rather not say more. But the town is small and the talk has spread, and it is better to set down plainly what was seen than to leave people guessing.

neutral.t: The two live in the same town, a few minutes' walk apart, and yet a letter goes every week. When what needs saying cannot be said face to face, that is an explanation in itself.
There is no law against a few words on a bridge at night. Keeping it from one's own family is another matter.

neutral: This paper does not judge who is right and who is wrong. Both households still live in this town, and how they go on from here is their own affair.

hot.t: The hardest part of this falls on the one who sits at home and waits.
A person with a home ought to be in it at night.

any.t: Walking together on the bridge may be chance. A letter every week is not.
Someone goes out at night; someone at home has wept more than once; someone else saw two people walking together on the bridge. Three different people tell it, and they tell the same story.
As for the talk that {lover.short} was paid to come here, this paper could not find one person able to say who paid. That much is idle talk.
This town has always held its schoolteachers to a stricter account than other people. That may not be fair to {target.short}.
{target.short} has taken the measurements of half the households in town. Knowing so many people means a great many tongues.
The lamp on the bridge burns all night, and anyone who passes is seen. Someone truly keeping a secret would not choose that spot; choosing it suggests they thought nobody would be about.
Of two people walking together at night, this paper can write only what was seen. What was said and where they went, this paper does not know and will not guess.
The post office knows where every letter goes, but not what is in it. So it is with this paper.
A letter a week comes to fifty-odd in a year. An ordinary acquaintance does not run to so many.
The suspicion came from within the family itself, and this paper has not asked what is suspected. The town need not guess on that family's behalf.
Someone who has wept more than once is not weeping over one late night.

{target.short} says the letters are about nothing but ordinary business.

calm: This paper will write no more about it.
